final_text:
I couldn't diagnose your regression, and I want to be straight about why: the workspace was empty — no repo, no metrics, no logs, no service. So anything I named as "the cause" would have been invented. What I built instead is the shortest path from one sentence ("p95 doubled after the last release") to a cause, with the branches that actually change what you do.

**Two decisions come before any diagnosis, and they're independent:**

1. **Roll back, or diagnose in place.** Roll back if the SLO is breached for real users, if error/timeout/retry counts are climbing (they compound), or if versions are mixed and you have no clean pre/post split. Rollback isn't only mitigation — it's your strongest experiment. If p95 recovers, the release is causal and you bisect a known-bad range. If it doesn't recover, the release was never the cause (traffic shift, a degraded dependency, or the measurement itself), and you've saved days.
2. **Is the latency real, or is the measurement?** ~15 minutes, highest yield, and the most common false alarm — because instrumentation ships *with* releases. Changed histogram bucket boundaries can double a computed p95 with zero behaviour change (p95 is interpolated between edges). So can averaging per-minute p95s instead of the pool's, moving the timer client-side, adding a proxy hop, or a silently changed timeout default.

**Then read the shape, not the number.** p50 flat + p95 doubled means a subset or a tail mechanism. Everything up together means a uniform slowdown. p95 moved but p99 barely did means a new slow cohort sitting right at the 95th percentile — very typical of a partially rolled-out version. p95 pinned at an exact round number is a timeout, not a speed problem. The arithmetic that matters: p95 is a boundary, not an average, so a cohort of a few percent of traffic moving several times slower shifts p95 while p50 never budges — "p50 is fine" never rules out a real regression.

Only after that does the order tracing → profiling → ablation apply, and each step has an entry condition: tracing tells you *which* span moved (diff span breakdowns above p95, before vs after — you want the span whose delta equals the added time, not the biggest span); profiling tells you *why* that span is slow, and is close to useless before a hotspot is located; ablation confirms whether a component earns its place and needs a fixed workload plus a quality metric, because a change can be fast and wrong.

The runbook with the slicing checklist, the PromQL starting point, the timeline for confirming with a canary, and the five things I'd need to make this specific is here: [p95-regression-triage.md](p95-regression-triage.md).

**Verified:** only that the workspace was empty — nothing above is a measurement of your service, and no numbers were fabricated. **Not verified:** where your latency actually went; every "where to look" entry is a hypothesis ranked by base rate. Send me pre/post p50/p95/p99/RPS/error for a week either side and whether the change was a step or a ramp, and this collapses to one branch.

p95-does-not-give-me-a-cause task, done. Workspace <SCRATCH>/Mo7qxduj was EMPTY (no repo, no metrics, no logs), so I did not invent a diagnosis. Deliverable: <SCRATCH>/Mo7qxduj/p95-regression-triage.md — a triage runbook with the decision branches.

CORE ANSWER, in the order it must be executed:

Step 0 — two decisions before any diagnosis.
(a) Roll back / flag off, or diagnose in place? Roll back if the SLO is breached for real users, error/timeout/retry counts are rising (they compound), or versions are mixed so no clean pre/post split exists. Key point: rollback is not just mitigation, it is the strongest experiment — if p95 recovers, the release is causal and you bisect a known-bad range; if it does not recover, the release was never the cause (traffic shift, degraded dependency, or measurement change) and you have saved days. Exception: don't roll back blindly over an irreversible migration.
(b) Is the latency real, or is the measurement? ~15 min, highest-yield check, because instrumentation ships WITH releases: changed histogram bucket boundaries (p95 is interpolated between edges, so re-bucketing can double it with zero behaviour change), averaging per-minute or per-instance p95s instead of the pool's p95, timer moved server→client or a new proxy hop, new sampling/tracing, changed timeout/retry defaults, unit or label change.

Step 1 — read the distribution shape, not the number. p50 flat + p95 doubled = a subset/tail mechanism. All quantiles up together = uniform slowdown (shared dependency, added synchronous call, capacity). p95 moved but p99 barely moved = a new slow cohort sitting at the 95th percentile, which is very typical of a partially rolled-out version. p95 pinned at an exact round number = timeout/deadline, not speed. Bimodal histogram = two populations (cache hit/miss, warm/cold, old/new build). Also check RPS and error rate: RPS up with latency = saturation, possibly not a code regression at all. Arithmetic that matters: p95 is a boundary, not an average — a cohort of a few percent of traffic, several times slower, moves p95 while p50 never budges. So "p50 is fine" never rules out a real regression.

Step 2 — localize by slicing the same window, cheapest dimension first: version/build SHA first (rolling deploy means old and new serve simultaneously; 10% of traffic on a slow new build puts p95 in the gap), then route/endpoint, instance/pod/AZ, status code, payload size/request class, upstream dependency latency. Included a PromQL starting point using histogram_quantile with `le`+`version` labels. If there is no `version` label, that gap is the first thing to fix.

Step 3 — tracing: WHERE the time goes. Diff span breakdowns of traces above p95 before vs after (look for the span whose DELTA equals the added time, not the biggest span), and separately slow-vs-fast within the after window. Watch for a newly added span (sync call, retry attempt, N+1, cache now missing). If no span accounts for the delta, that is a finding, not a dead end: queueing before the handler, connection/TLS setup, GC, thread-pool wait, or the measurement itself.

Step 4 — profiling: WHY that span is slow, and only after step 3 located it. CPU (perf/pprof/async-profiler/py-spy) for CPU-bound; off-CPU, lock contention, allocation/GC, pool wait for the rest. Diff old vs new build; an absolute profile is much weaker than a profile difference.

Step 5 — ablation: does the suspect earn its place. Confirmation, not discovery: revert only the suspect change in a canary. Needs fixed representative workload, repeated runs, and a quality metric as well as latency — a change can be fast and wrong.

Step 6 — confirm with a canary (previous build vs new on identical infra/traffic; a plain rollback does not separate code from environment) and bisect inside the known-bad range. Prevention: p95/p99 split by version on the release dashboard, canary with automatic rollback on p95 regression (latency regressions rarely page anyone), load-test gate with a recorded baseline, one behavioural change per deploy counting config and dependency bumps as changes.

VERIFIED / NOT VERIFIED — state this if you relay it: verified is only that the workspace was empty, so nothing above is a measurement of their service; the runbook is a method, and every "where to look" entry is a hypothesis ranked by base rate, not a finding. No numbers were fabricated; the only arithmetic offered is about how quantiles behave, which is definitional.

WHAT WOULD COLLAPSE THE PLAN TO ONE BRANCH (asking the user): (1) pre/post p50/p95/p99/RPS/error/timeout for one week either side; (2) step change or gradual, and is it still deployed; (3) is rollback cheap and safe (irreversible migration?); (4) stack and where the p95 comes from (APM? which aggregation?); (5) what shipped that touches the request hot path — code, config, dependency bumps, instance type, feature flags, DB migration, log level, sampling. Note the framing question too: "doubled" from 40ms to 80ms and from 400ms to 800ms call for different urgency.

The single most important thing not to do: start from a list of optimizations. Without a span delta you do not know which part moved, and the two cheapest actions (rollback, measurement check) both come before any profiling.
